label: Unit 1
themeSub: Naming them by the job they do, and measuring before you cut
intro: Every other track here happens on a screen. This one doesn't work at all unless something real ends up in his hands — the games are the backup, the tool drawer is the lesson. Four is old enough for a tape measure, a screwdriver and safety glasses; what he can't do yet is choose which one, so naming tools by their job comes before using them. Measuring is the same idea from the other end: a number is how big a thing actually is, not a word you say while you count. And these are the jobs a machine isn't taking. Writing the code turns out to be the easy part — getting under the sink is not.

gelds.text: Names six tools and says the job each one does
Chooses a tool before starting, and says why that one
Turns a screw the tightening way without being told which
Guesses how big something is, then measures it and reads the number
Knows which tools are his and which he has to ask for

tryNote: Ten minutes with a real screwdriver and a loose cabinet handle beats every game on this page. Let him pick the wrong tool first — the wrong one teaches what the right one is for.

daily.title: He picks the tool
daily.do: Find a real job that takes five minutes — a loose handle, a battery cover, a picture to hang. Put four tools on the table, all of them ones he's allowed to hold, and let him choose before you start. Then do the job with whatever he picked.
daily.stretch: Ask why that one, before he picks it up. A wrong pick that gets tried and doesn't work teaches the job of the tool better than being handed the right one.
daily.skill: Matching a tool to the job

daily.title: Guess, then measure
daily.do: Tape measure out. Pick something — the table, his foot, the dog if it'll hold still. He guesses how long it is, then you measure it together and say the number out loud.
daily.stretch: Guess first every time, then say whether the guess was over or under. The guess is what turns the number into information instead of a noise.
daily.skill: A number is how big a thing is

daily.title: Which way tightens
daily.do: Shampoo caps, the tap, a jar lid off the side. Righty-tighty, lefty-loosey — say it every time, and let him do the turning.
daily.stretch: He calls which way BEFORE he turns it. Calling it first is the difference between knowing it and finding out.

goalsTitle: What he should have by the end of this unit

his: Names hammer, screwdriver, saw, tape measure, wrench and clamp
Hands you the right tool when you say what the job is
Reads a number off a tape measure and says it out loud
Says righty-tighty and turns the correct way
Asks before touching the saw, the drill or the tall ladder
Checks in an order when something won't work — on, plugged in, broken

weekend: Find one broken thing in the house and fix it with him, start to finish — measure, pick the tool, do the job, put the tools away. He's the one who says when it's done.

songs.title: Every Tool Has a Job
songs.style: A cheerful preschool workshop sing-along with woodblock taps, acoustic guitar and hand claps. Slow, steady tempo a four-year-old can sing with, one warm friendly voice, a simple repeated melody, every word clear. Singing starts within the first two seconds, and it ends cleanly with no long outro.
lyrics: The hammer taps the nails in —
The tape measure tells the number
so I know just what to do.
I measure twice, I ask first,
and I can name them all. I will!

advanced.label: Tape measure
advanced.note: A tape measure tells you how big something is before you cut it.

advanced.label: Wrench
advanced.note: A wrench grips a nut and turns it, because your fingers aren't strong enough.

advanced.label: Clamp
advanced.note: A clamp is a second pair of hands. It holds the thing still while you work on it.

advanced.label: Bolt
advanced.note: A bolt goes through the hole, and a nut spins onto the end to hold it there.

advanced.label: Safety glasses
advanced.note: Glasses go on before anything starts flying about.

advanced.label: Toolbox
advanced.note: A toolbox is why you can find the right tool instead of hunting for it.

advanced.label: Pencil
advanced.note: The pencil marks where to cut. Measure, mark, then cut.

advanced.label: Flashlight
advanced.note: A flashlight lights up the dark spot under the sink, so you can see what you're fixing.

sort.title: Mine or a Grown-Up's?
sort.sub: Which ones can he pick up
sort.noSay: Right. That one you ask for.
sort.retry: Could it cut you, burn you, or drop you? Have another go.

items.note: Yours to pull out and read. Walk it back in with your hand — a blade let go snaps back and catches fingers.
Teeth that cut through wood cut through a hand exactly as well.
Sweeping up is part of the job, not the punishment after it.
A grown-up's, every time. It spins faster than you can let go.
Always yours. They go on before anybody starts.
Yours, with somebody standing next to you. Eyes on the nail, and the other hand well out of the way.
Anything that puts your head higher than a grown-up's is theirs.
One step up is yours. The tall ladder still isn't.
Slow, and all it does is turn. The safest real tool in the drawer.
It says glue, and glue is yours — but this one burns you before you feel it.
It fires nails into wood with a bang. Not even a big kid's.
Yours. The mess is the grown-up's problem.

items.text: The grey box on the wall with all the switches.
items.note: Nobody opens that but Dad. Every bit of electricity in the house comes through there.
Heavy, but it can't cut you or spin on its own. Yours if you can lift it.
Yours. Marking the line is your job on every cut.
Spinning blades under a lid. Not yours until you're much bigger.
Rough on purpose, and it only rubs. Yours, with your glasses on and somebody next to you, and you'll know it's working when you see the dust.
A blade that slides out when you push. A grown-up's, always.

sort.title: Measure It or Just Look?
sort.sub: Does this one need a number?
sort.yesSay: Yes. That one needs a number.
sort.noSay: Right. You can just look at that one.
sort.retry: Would it matter if you got it a bit wrong? Have another go.

items.text: A shelf that has to fit inside a cupboard.
items.note: A little bit too long and it doesn't go in at all.
Look out the window. Done.

items.text: Cutting a piece of wood for a box.
items.note: Measure twice, cut once, because nobody has ever uncut anything.

items.text: Which of two apples is bigger.
items.note: You could measure it. You don't need to, and nothing goes wrong if you're off.
The number is the whole point, so he can beat it next year.
On or off. There's no number in it.

items.text: A rug to go under the table.
items.note: Rugs come in sizes, and a wrong one is a long drive back to the shop.
The one on this list where guessing is actually dangerous.
Baking is measuring. That's most of what baking is.

items.text: Whether the dog wants to go out.
items.note: He'll tell you.
Too short is a curtain you can see under all winter.
You look. Nobody in history has measured a bath.

items.text: Whether the sofa will fit through the door.
items.note: Everybody thinks they can eyeball this one. Everybody is wrong.
You know your own shoes by looking at them.
Feet have a number. Guess it and you limp all week.
Look in it. Done.

items.text: How long to cook the egg.
items.note: Time is a measurement too. A minute off and it's a different egg.
Look out the window. There's no number in it.

steps.text: Mark the spot with a pencil
Step back and check it's straight
Get the screwdriver that fits it
Turn it to the right until it stops

sets.goal: When the lamp won't turn on

steps.text: Switch it off and pull the plug out
Now it's safe to try another bulb
Tell a grown-up what you already checked
Measure how long it needs to be
Draw the line to cut on
A grown-up saws along the line
Push down on each corner and find the wobble
Set it back on its feet
Push on it again — no wobble

sets.goal: Putting a new battery in the torch

steps.text: New battery in, the right way round
Wipe it on the edge of the tin
Sweep the bits off the floor
Every tool back in the box
